title: the Pandavas' last journey, Yudhishthira's dog, heaven
hook: at the top of the world, a god offers Yudhishthira heaven, on one condition: leave the dog behind
carry: he will not give it up
tomorrow: the Pandavas' last journey, Yudhishthira's dog, heaven

segments.voice: Yesterday on the Pandavas' last journey, Arjuna fell, then Bhima, and Yudhishthira walked on with only the dog. Your line was you ate without a thought for others. Did you set down one small weight? Day eight hundred seventy-seven.
screen: `THE LAST JOURNEY.` · `ONE BY ONE THEY FALL.`

segments.voice: Two of them are left on the mountain: a king and a dog. Yudhishthira's brothers have fallen behind him. Draupadi has fallen. The dog that joined them at the start of the road has not. It is still at his heel. Then the sky fills with sound, and Indra, king of the gods, pulls up in a chariot and tells Yudhishthira to climb in. Heaven is waiting. This is the moment the whole road has been leading to. And in Ganguli's telling, Yudhishthira's first answer is not yes. It's a question about who gets to come with him.
screen: `A KING AND A DOG.` → `INDRA'S CHARIOT ARRIVES.` → `"CLIMB IN."`

segments.voice: First he asks about his brothers and Draupadi. He won't go without them. Indra reassures him: they are already in heaven. They left their bodies on the way. You, he says, will go up in yours. So far, good news. Then Yudhishthira says the dog has been devoted to him, and it should come too. And Indra says no. You have won heaven and a state like a god's, he says. Leave the dog. There is no cruelty in that. Heaven has no place for people with dogs. Notice how reasonable it sounds. It's only a dog. The offer is enormous. And there is no one to speak for the dog but him. Yudhishthira refuses. In the text he says that turning away one who is devoted to you, who is frightened and has nowhere else to go, is a grave wrong, and that he will not give it up even for his own happiness. Heaven or no heaven, the dog stays with him. Then the dog changes. It is Dharma, the god of righteousness, Yudhishthira's own father, who has been walking beside him in disguise. Dharma praises him. He reminds his son of an earlier test, in the forest, at a lake, when Yudhishthira was asked to choose one brother to bring back to life and chose Nakula, the son of his other mother, out of fairness. Now he has chosen again, for a dog. Only then does Yudhishthira climb into the chariot. The epic was long and full of wars. This examination turns out to be very small: whether a king will keep faith with a creature that can't repay him.
screen: `"NOT WITHOUT MY BROTHERS"` · `INDRA: LEAVE THE DOG` · `"I WILL NOT TURN IT AWAY"` · then, large: `THE DOG IS DHARMA`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let your breath slow down. Bring to mind a creature or a person who depends on you and can't give much back. A pet. A small child. A parent who needs more help now. Breathe in and simply see them near you. Breathe out and let your shoulders soften. You don't have to promise anything. Just notice that they're still there. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Dharma. The god of righteousness, who walked beside Yudhishthira the whole way as a dog, and revealed himself only at the gate of heaven.
Your line: he will not give it up. Today, do one small kindness for someone who has stuck with you and can't repay it. Day eight hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: The story of Yudhishthira and the dog comes from the Mahaprasthanika Parva of the Mahabharata; Hindus hear it in recitations and retellings of the epic, and some retellers draw from it a lesson in loyalty and dharma.

match.prompt: at heaven's door — tap the pairs.

myth: Indra tells Yudhishthira his brothers are lost
he says they are already in heaven, having left their bodies on the way.
the dog turns out to be Yudhishthira's father
it is Dharma, the god of righteousness, who fathered Yudhishthira.
Yudhishthira agrees to leave the dog once heaven is offered
he refuses, and only climbs in after the dog reveals itself.

fork.setup: you're Yudhishthira. a god offers you heaven right now, if you leave behind the dog that has followed you the whole way. what do you do?
options: climb in; it's only a dog.
refuse to go without the dog.
ask the dog to wait for you.
fork.reveal: he refuses to turn away one who is devoted and frightened, and the dog reveals itself as Dharma, his father.

original.note: dharma: the god of righteousness, who walks beside Yudhishthira as the dog.

trapdoor: what you thought: a king gets to heaven by winning a great war.
what it means: at heaven's door he is told to leave a dog behind, and he won't.
what a scholar hears: the dog is Dharma, and the scene echoes the earlier test at the lake, where Yudhishthira chose fairly for Nakula.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Mahaprasthanika Parva, closing section: Indra's chariot, the question of the brothers, the dog, Dharma revealed
Mahabharata, Vana Parva, the Yaksha's questions at the lake (recalled by Dharma)

notes: All paraphrase of Ganguli. Lines in quotation marks on screen are plain-English glosses of speech, not quotations.
Confirm Indra's reply that the brothers and Draupadi have gone ahead having cast off their bodies, while Yudhishthira ascends in his own body.

Confirm the gloss of Yudhishthira's refusal (abandoning one who is devoted, frightened and without other refuge is a grave wrong; he will not abandon it for his own happiness). Ganguli compares the sin to slaying a brahmana; that comparison was left out here.
Confirm Indra's line that heaven has no place for persons with dogs, and that he says there is no cruelty in leaving it.
Confirm that Dharma recalls the earlier test at the lake in the Dvaita forest, where Yudhishthira chose Nakula for the sake of Madri.
Day 876 ends with the falls of Arjuna and Bhima and the dog still following; the review now picks that up.
